steps.title: Water mass per unit volume
steps.why: Ice fills the fraction $\phi$ of each small volume and gas fills $1-\phi$. So the water mass per unit total volume is the ice mass plus the vapor mass held in the gas.
steps.operation: definition of mixture mass density from volume fractions

check.printed: no tools in this run; by hand, both terms are in kg m^-3

steps.title: Integral conservation of water
steps.why: Water is neither created nor destroyed (A5), so in a fixed control volume its mass changes only through flux across the boundary. Ice does not move (A2), so only vapor carries a flux.
steps.operation: mass balance on a fixed control volume

check.printed: no tools in this run; by hand, both sides are in kg s^-1

steps.title: Local conservation law
steps.why: The fields are smooth (A1), so the time derivative can move inside the integral and the divergence theorem turns the surface integral into a volume integral. Because $\Omega$ is arbitrary, the integrand must vanish.
steps.operation: divergence theorem and arbitrariness of the control volume

check.printed: no tools in this run; by hand, every term is in kg m^-3 s^-1. The constant $\rho_i$ (A2) is pulled out of $\partial_t(\rho_i\phi)$

steps.title: Fickian vapor flux in the gas fraction
steps.why: Vapor diffuses only through the gas, which fills the fraction $1-\phi$ of each volume. With Fick's law in the gas (A3) and no net gas flow (A4), the flux per unit total area is the gas fraction times the Fickian flux.
steps.operation: constitutive law (Fick) weighted by gas fraction

check.printed: no tools in this run; by hand, units are m^2 s^-1 times kg m^-4, which is kg m^-2 s^-1

steps.title: Vapor equation as R = 0
steps.why: Substituting S4 into S3 and writing the divergence in Cartesian components gives the residual. The term $\rho_i\partial_t\phi$ is the exchange with ice: deposition ($\partial_t\phi>0$) removes vapor and sublimation adds it.
steps.operation: substitution of S4 into S3, Cartesian divergence

check.printed: no tools in this run; by hand, every term is in kg m^-3 s^-1

assumptions_used: A1: $\phi(x,y,z,t)$ and $T(x,y,z,t)$ are known, smooth fields (given).
A2: Ice is a rigid, immobile solid with constant density $\rho_i$ (no ice velocity, no thermal expansion).
A3: Vapor moves through the gas by Fickian diffusion with diffusivity $D_v(T)$. Any dependence on gas pressure is absorbed into $D_v$.
A4: The gas has no net bulk flow, so there is no advection term.
A5: No water enters or leaves except through the vapor flux, and there is no liquid water. Water mass is conserved.

neglected.effect: Advection of vapor by bulk gas flow (including the Stefan flow at the interface)
neglected.why: The vapor is very dilute near 200 K (vapor pressure about 0.16 Pa, so $\rho_v$ is about 1e-6 kg m^-3), so the Stefan velocity is about $D_v\nabla\rho_v/\rho_{gas}$ and is negligible compared with diffusion. There is no imposed pressure gradient across the pores.

neglected.effect: Thermal diffusion (the Soret effect) and cross-diffusion
neglected.why: The thermal diffusion factor for water in air is about 0.1 or less. Over pore-scale temperature differences of about 1 K at 200 K, it contributes a flux of order 1e-3 of the Fickian flux.

This is valid only while the mean free path is smaller than the pore size. Under lunar near-vacuum it is not, and then $D_v$ must be replaced by a Knudsen diffusivity. The form of the equation stays the same.

neglected.effect: Variation of ice density with temperature, and ice motion
neglected.why: The thermal expansion of ice is about 5e-5 per K, so changes in $\rho_i$ are about 1e-4 of $\rho_i$. Grains are assumed fixed.

neglected.effect: Liquid water and adsorbed water on regolith grains
neglected.why: Near 200 K there is no liquid phase. Adsorption on the grain surfaces is outside the ice/gas model.

questions: Should the vapor flux carry the gas-fraction weighting $(1-\phi)$, as used here so that water mass is conserved exactly? The alternative is the common simplified form $\partial_t\rho_v = \nabla\cdot(D_v\nabla\rho_v) - \rho_i\partial_t\phi$.
